1.note: The original language uses a cardinal number, **one**, where your language might use an ordinal number. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **In the year of one to Darius**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the first year of Darius]

1.q: בֶּן־אֲחַשְׁוֵר֖וֹשׁ מִ⁠זֶּ֣רַע מָדָ֑י אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָמְלַ֔ךְ עַ֖ל מַלְכ֥וּת כַּשְׂדִּֽים
1.note: Daniel is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Daniel is speaking as if Darius were **seed** that had come from Madai. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a descendant of Madai]

The expression **who had been made king** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [who reigned as king]

1.q: בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת אַחַ֗ת לְ⁠דָרְיָ֛וֶשׁ בֶּן־אֲחַשְׁוֵר֖וֹשׁ מִ⁠זֶּ֣רַע מָדָ֑י אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָמְלַ֔ךְ עַ֖ל מַלְכ֥וּת כַּשְׂדִּֽים
1.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine [9:1](ta:09) and 9:2 into a verse bridge, as the UST does, in order to keep the information about the date of Darius’s reign together.

2.note: The implication is that **the scrolls** were the writings of the prophets. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [perceived in the sacred scrolls written by the prophets]

2.q: מִסְפַּ֣ר הַ⁠שָּׁנִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָיָ֤ה דְבַר־יְהוָה֙ אֶל־יִרְמִיָ֣ה הַ⁠נָּבִ֔יא לְ⁠מַלֹּ֛אות לְ⁠חָרְב֥וֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה
2.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **seventy years** with the information about **the number of years**. Alternate translation: [the number of years, seventy of them, that was the word of Yahweh to Jeremiah the prophet for the filling of the desolations of Jerusalem]

Daniel is using **the filling of the desolations of Jerusalem** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the completion of the years during which Jerusalem would lie in ruins.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the completion of the time during which Jerusalem would lie in ruins]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the days in which Jerusalem would lie devastated]

3.note: Daniel is using **I set my face to the Lord God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I gave my full attention to the Lord God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I turned my full attention to the Lord God]

The terms **prayer** and **supplications** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [by earnest pleading]

Going without food, wearing rough cloth, and putting ashes on oneself were symbolic actions by which Daniel showed that he was mourning over sin and humbling himself before God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [with fasting and sackcloth and ashes to show that I was mourning and humbling myself]

In this verse, the word **ashes** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the particles of ashes as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “ashes.” Alternate translation: [and ash particles]

4.note: Daniel is using three verbs, **I prayed**, **I confessed**, and **said**, to introduce a single direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Daniel is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of urgent appeal to God. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Please, Lord]

The terms **great** and **feared** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the awesome God]

The terms **keeping covenant** and **covenant faithfulness** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the one faithfully keeping his covenant]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant** and **faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [what he promised, and acting faithfully]

Even though Daniel is addressing God directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **him** and **his** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [to the ones loving you and to the keepers of your commandments]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [to the ones who show that they truly love him by keeping his commandments]

5.note: By **we**, Daniel means himself and his fellow Israelites but not the one to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and acted perversely]

Daniel is speaking as if refusing to obey God’s commands were **turning away** from them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [refusing to obey your commandments and your judgments]

The terms **your commandments** and **your judgments** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [turning away from all of your laws]

6.note: Daniel is using **we have not listened to** as a common expression of the culture to mean “we have not obeyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And we have not obeyed your servants the prophets]

Here, **your name** represents “your authority.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who spoke by your authority]

Daniel is speaking as if all of the earlier generations of the Israelites were their **fathers**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and our forefathers]

7.note: Daniel is using this expression as a common expression of the culture to mean “You, Lord, have always done what is right.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You, Lord, have always done what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [belong faces that show we are ashamed]

Daniel is using **faces** to represent the whole person who is ashamed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is complete disgrace]

Daniel is using **as this day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “as is the case at the present time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as is the case at the present time]

In this verse, the word **man** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the people of Judah as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “man.” Alternate translation: [to the men of Judah]

Daniel is using the adjectives **near** and **far** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the ones who are nearby and the ones who are far away]

It might seem that the expression **where you have driven them there** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [in all of the lands to which you have driven them]

8.note: Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to our kings, our princes, and our fathers there is also complete disgrace]

9.q: לַֽ⁠אדֹנָ֣⁠י אֱלֹהֵ֔י⁠נוּ הָ⁠רַחֲמִ֖ים וְ⁠הַ⁠סְּלִח֑וֹת כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְנוּ בּֽ⁠וֹ
9.note: Even though Daniel is addressing God directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **the Lord our God** and **him** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [To you, our Lord and God, we pray for compassion and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against you]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **compassion** and **forgiveness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [we ask that you would act compassionately and forgive us]

10.note: Here, **the voice of Yahweh our God** represents “what Yahweh our God commanded.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to what Yahweh our God commanded]

Daniel is speaking as if obeying God’s laws were **to walk in** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to obey his laws]
Here, **our faces** represents “us.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [that he gave to us]

Here, **the hand** represents the agency of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [through his servants the prophets]

11.q: וַ⁠תִּתַּ֨ךְ עָלֵ֜י⁠נוּ הָ⁠אָלָ֣ה וְ⁠הַ⁠שְּׁבֻעָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר כְּתוּבָה֙ בְּ⁠תוֹרַת֙ מֹשֶׁ֣ה
11.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the curse** with the information about **the oath**. Alternate translation: [And the oath and the curse have been poured out on us, which are written in the law of Moses]

Daniel is speaking as if the oath and the curse were a liquid that could be **poured out** on the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And we have experienced the oath and the curse]

The expression **has been poured out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And you have poured out the oath]

The expression **that is written** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that God had written]

12.note: Daniel is using **made stand his word** as a common expression of the culture to mean “fulfilled his word.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [kept his word] or [done what he said he would do]

12.q: אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא־נֶעֶשְׂתָ֗ה תַּ֚חַת כָּל־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר נֶעֶשְׂתָ֖ה בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
12.note: The expressions **has not been done** and **has been done** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that he has not done anywhere under all of the heavens like what he has done to Jerusalem]

13.note: Daniel is using **the face** to represent Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but we have not entreated Yahweh our God himself]

Daniel is speaking as if abandoning sin were **to return from** a place where the people had been. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to turn away from our iniquities] or [to repent of our sin]

14.note: Daniel is using **Yahweh watched over the trouble** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh kept the disaster ready to send.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh watched for the right time to bring the disaster]

15.note: The words **And now** mark a transition from Daniel’s confession to his request. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [So then, Lord our God]
Here, **a mighty hand** represents “great power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with your mighty strength]

Here, **a name** represents “a reputation.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and made a reputation for yourself]

16.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousnesses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to your righteous deeds]

The phrase **according to all of your righteousnesses** probably refers initially to Yahweh’s “righteous acts,” that is, his acts of deliverance, supremely in the Exodus, described in v. 15. But in light of the overall prayer, it also refers to his righteous character (vv. 7, 14). This phrase could mean: (1) [in keeping with your acts of deliverance] or (2) [because you always do what is right]

The implication is that **your righteousnesses** are the righteous deeds by which Yahweh had rescued his people in the past. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to all of the righteous deeds by which you have rescued us in the past]

Daniel is using **your nose and your heat** as a common expression of the culture to mean “your burning anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you please turn your fierce anger away]

Daniel is using the possessive form to describe a **mountain** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your holy mountain]

The implication is that **the mountain of your holiness** is Mount Zion, where the temple stood. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [your holy mountain, Mount Zion]

17.note: Even though Daniel is speaking about himself, he refers to himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility before God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [listen to my prayer, your servant, and to my supplications]

Daniel is speaking as if Yahweh’s favor were light shining from his **face** onto the sanctuary. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and show your favor to your desolate sanctuary]

Even though Daniel is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **the Lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [for your own sake, my Lord]

18.note: Daniel is using **Incline your ear** as a common expression of the culture to mean “please give me your attention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention, my God, and hear]

Daniel is using **Open your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “pay attention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention and consider]

The phrase **our desolations and the city upon which your name is called** expresses a single idea. The word **desolations** describes the state of **the city**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [the desolations of our city, upon which your name is called] or [the city upon which your name is called, which lies in desolation]

The expression **your name is called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the city upon which you have put your name]

Daniel is using **the city upon which your name is called** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the city that is your own possession.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the city that is your own possession]

Daniel is using **making our supplications fall to your face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “presenting our requests to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are not laying our petitions before you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mercies**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how very merciful you are]

19.q: אֲדֹנָ֤⁠י ׀ שְׁמָ֨עָ⁠ה֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י ׀ סְלָ֔חָ⁠ה אֲדֹנָ֛⁠י הַֽקֲשִׁ֥יבָ⁠ה וַ⁠עֲשֵׂ֖ה
19.note: The words translated as **hear**, **forgive**, **pay attention** and **act** are imperatives, but they communicate a request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [Lord, I ask you to hear! Lord, I beg you to forgive! Lord, I plead with you to pay attention and act]

20.q: וְ⁠ע֨וֹד אֲנִ֤י מְדַבֵּר֙ וּ⁠מִתְפַּלֵּ֔ל וּ⁠מִתְוַדֶּה֙ חַטָּאתִ֔⁠י וְ⁠חַטַּ֖את עַמִּ֣⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וּ⁠מַפִּ֣יל תְּחִנָּתִ֗⁠י לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהַ֔⁠י עַ֖ל הַר־קֹ֥דֶשׁ אֱלֹהָֽ⁠י
20.note: You can create a verse bridge for these two verses, 20-21, in order not to repeat the information “I was still speaking.” The UST models one way to do that.

20.q: וְ⁠ע֨וֹד אֲנִ֤י מְדַבֵּר֙ וּ⁠מִתְפַּלֵּ֔ל וּ⁠מִתְוַדֶּה֙ חַטָּאתִ֔⁠י וְ⁠חַטַּ֖את עַמִּ֣⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וּ⁠מַפִּ֣יל תְּחִנָּתִ֗⁠י לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהַ֔⁠י עַ֖ל הַר־קֹ֥דֶשׁ אֱלֹהָֽ⁠י
20.note: The words that the ULT translates as **And I was still speaking** indicate that Gabriel came to Daniel at the same time as when Daniel was praying. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [While I was still speaking and praying and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel and presenting my supplication before Yahweh my God for the holy mountain of my God]

21.q: וְ⁠הָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ גַּבְרִיאֵ֡ל אֲשֶׁר֩ רָאִ֨יתִי בֶ⁠חָז֤וֹן בַּ⁠תְּחִלָּה֙
21.note: Daniel is reintroducing **the man Gabriel**, whom he had described earlier, as a participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of reintroducing participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and Gabriel, the same man whom I had seen earlier in the vision]

The implication is that Gabriel was an angel, and Daniel calls him **the man** because Gabriel appeared in human form. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the angel Gabriel]

The implication is that **the offering of the evening** was the sacrifice that the priests offered every day at that time. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the time when the priests presented the daily evening sacrifice]

22.note: Daniel is describing one event, Gabriel making him understand, before describing another event that preceded it, Gabriel speaking with him. If it would be helpful in your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened, as in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **understanding**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to enable you to understand wisely]

23.note: The implication is that **a word came forth** from God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a word came forth from God]

Gabriel is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I have come** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself has come immediately to answer Daniel’s prayer. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I have indeed come]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desirablenesses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for you are very precious]

Gabriel is using the term **desirablenesses** as a common expression of the culture to mean “one whom God loves greatly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for you are one whom God loves greatly]

In the original language, the first **understand** is “Qal,” and the second **understand** is from “Hiphil.” The meaning of the second is not to “make understood” but ingressive, to “come to understand.” Some languages may have forms that they can use to express these slightly different meanings. Alternate translation: [So consider this message and grasp the meaning of this vision] or [Therefore, ponder the message and begin to understand the meaning of the vision]

24.note: The expression **have been determined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God has determined seventy sevens]

The expression **Seventy sevens** refers to seventy units of seven. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Seventy periods of seven]

24.q: לְ⁠כַלֵּ֨א הַ⁠פֶּ֜שַׁע ו⁠ל⁠חתם חטאות וּ⁠לְ⁠כַפֵּ֣ר עָוֺ֔ן וּ⁠לְ⁠הָבִ֖יא צֶ֣דֶק עֹֽלָמִ֑ים
24.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **transgression**, **sins**, **iniquity**, and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [to stop people from transgressing and to seal up what they have done wrongly and to cover what they have done perversely and to bring in what is eternally right]

Gabriel is speaking as if putting an end to sins were **to seal up** a container so that nothing more could come out of it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to put an end to sins]

Gabriel is speaking as if forgiving iniquity were **to cover** it so that it could no longer be seen. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to forgive iniquity]

Gabriel is speaking as if bringing about what the prophets foretold were **to seal up** a document to certify it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to fulfill vision and prophecy]

This could mean: (1) **the Holy of Holies** refers to the most holy place in the temple or (2) it refers to a most holy person. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and to anoint the most holy place in the temple]

25.note: The terms **know** and **understand** mean similar things. Gabriel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And may you understand this clearly]

Gabriel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [from the time when a king issues the command to return and to build Jerusalem]

The implication is that **the going forth of the word** is the issuing of a royal decree. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the issuing of the royal decree]
Here **return** is an idiom meaning “do again.” Alternate translation: [to build Jerusalem again] or [to rebuild Jerusalem]

As in the instance of “return” earlier in this verse, here **It will return and it will be built** means “It will be built again.” Alternate translation: [It will be built again] or [It will be rebuilt]
The expression **sixty and two** describes a single number. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [sixty-two]
The pronoun **It** refers to Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Jerusalem will return]

The expression **it will be built** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will build it with a square and a trench]

Gabriel is using the possessive form to describe **times** that are characterized by **distress**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but in distressful times]

26.note: The expression **will be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies will cut off the anointed one]

Gabriel is speaking as if the killing of the anointed one were his being **cut off**, as a branch is cut from a tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the anointed one will be killed]

Gabriel is using this expression as a common expression of the culture to mean that the anointed one would be left with nothing. This could mean that he would have (1) no possessions or (2) no one to support him. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will have nothing]

26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the people of the coming ruler** before the information about **the city and the sanctuary**. Alternate translation: [And the people of the coming ruler will destroy the city and the sanctuary]

This could mean: (1) **its** refers to the city or (2) it refers to the coming ruler. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the end of the city will be with a flood]

Gabriel is speaking as if the destruction that would come were **a flood** that would sweep everything away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it will come to an end in overwhelming destruction]

The expression **are determined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God has determined desolations]

27.note: This could mean: (1) **he** refers to the coming ruler or (2) it refers to the anointed one. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And that ruler will strengthen a covenant with many] or [And the anointed one will strengthen a covenant with many]

Gabriel is using **strengthen a covenant** as a common expression of the culture to mean “make a firm agreement.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will make a firm agreement with many]

Gabriel is using the adjective **many** as a noun to mean a certain group of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [with a large number of people]

The terms **the sacrifice** and **the offering** mean similar things. Gabriel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all the sacrifices]

Gabriel is speaking as if abominations were a creature with wings. This could mean: (1) **the wing of abominations** refers to the highest point of the temple, where something detestable would be set up, or (2) it refers to the extreme degree of the abominations that would be committed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And on the highest point of the temple, detestable things]

The implication is that **something making desolate** is a detestable object that would be set up in the temple. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will be placed a detestable object that makes the temple desolate]

The expressions **having been determined** and **will be poured out** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God will pour out upon the one desolating what he has determined]
